figures.title: The Processing Family Tree
figures.subtitle: What happens to food between farm and plate, in three groups.

segments.name: Processing
segments.text: This lesson is about processing: everything that happens to food between the farm and your plate. Almost every food is processed somehow, and this tree sorts what we'll cover into three groups.

segments.name: Unlisted Helpers
segments.text: On the left are processing aids, like the solvent hexane, which help make a food and then are removed, so they never reach the label.

segments.name: Made by Heat
segments.text: In the middle are compounds that form when food is heated hard. Browning makes acrylamide and AGEs, grilling and smoking make HCAs and PAHs, and curing plus frying makes nitrosamines.

segments.name: Changing the Food
segments.text: On the right are methods that change the food itself: fermenting, pasteurizing, hydrogenating, refining and nixtamalizing. Each box links to its figure.

segments.name: Good, Bad and Both
segments.text: Processing isn't good or bad as a whole. Pasteurizing and fermenting make food safer, nixtamalizing makes corn more nutritious, charring and partial hydrogenation make things worth limiting, and refining trades nutrients for shelf life.

figures.title: Processing Aids
figures.subtitle: Helpers like hexane that never reach the label.

segments.name: Hexane
segments.text: Here's hexane: six carbons in a row with nothing but hydrogens around them. With no oxygen, it mixes with oil, not water.

segments.name: Pulling Out Oil
segments.text: That's why it's used to make most soybean, canola, corn and sunflower oil. Crushed seeds are washed with hexane, which dissolves the oil out, and then the hexane is boiled off and recycled.

segments.name: How Much Is Left
segments.text: Hexane isn't a nutrient. Breathing high levels at work can damage nerves, but the traces left in oil are tiny; the EU caps them at one milligram per kilogram. Expeller-pressed, cold-pressed and USDA organic oils are made without it.

segments.name: Other Aids
segments.text: Other processing aids include enzymes that clear fruit juice, fining agents like gelatin or clay that pull haze out of wine and beer, anti-foaming agents, and carryover additives that came in with an ingredient.

segments.name: Why Not Listed
segments.text: US and EU rules let manufacturers leave these off the label when they're removed or do nothing in the final food. The exception is allergens: if an aid comes from fish, milk or another major allergen, it must still be declared.

figures.title: Browning: Acrylamide and AGEs
figures.subtitle: What forms when sugars meet amino acids in dry heat.

segments.name: Asparagine
segments.text: Browning starts with amino acids. Asparagine is plentiful in potatoes and grains. Heated above about 120 degrees Celsius with a sugar like glucose, it loses its amino-acid end.

segments.name: Acrylamide
segments.text: What's left is acrylamide: a reactive double bond next to the same amide group. It's part of the Maillard reaction, the browning that colors crusts, chips and coffee, and it was found in food in 2002.

segments.name: The Risk
segments.text: The body turns acrylamide into a compound that can damage DNA. It causes cancer in animals at high doses, and IARC calls it probably carcinogenic to humans. Studies in people haven't shown a clear link, but the advice is to fry, bake and toast to golden, not dark brown.

segments.name: Found In
segments.text: It's in fries, chips, crackers, cookies, toast, cereals and coffee. Boiled and steamed foods have essentially none.

segments.name: AGEs
segments.text: Sugars can also stick to proteins. Lysine's side chain ends in a free NH2 group, and after several steps it can carry this small acid group. That's carboxymethyl-lysine, the best-known AGE, or advanced glycation end product.

segments.name: AGEs in Food
segments.text: AGEs build up in the body with age and in diabetes, and food adds some, mostly from meat grilled, roasted or fried. How much food AGEs matter is still debated. Stewing, poaching and steaming make far fewer.

figures.title: Grilling and Smoking: HCAs and PAHs
figures.subtitle: Compounds made in charred meat and smoke.

segments.name: HCAs
segments.text: This is PhIP, a heterocyclic amine, or HCA: rings containing nitrogen with an amino group. HCAs form when creatine, amino acids and sugar in muscle meat react at very high heat.

segments.name: HCA Risk
segments.text: The liver activates HCAs into forms that damage DNA, and IARC lists PhIP as possibly carcinogenic. The National Cancer Institute suggests avoiding direct flame, turning meat often, and cutting off charred parts.

segments.name: PAHs
segments.text: Benzo a pyrene is a PAH: five benzene rings fused into one flat sheet. PAHs form when fat drips onto flames and the smoke coats the food.

segments.name: PAH Risk
segments.text: IARC classifies benzo a pyrene as carcinogenic to humans, and the EU limits it in smoked foods. Trim fat, avoid flare-ups, and scrape off char. Cigarette smoke is a far bigger source than food.

segments.name: Smoke Flavor
segments.text: Guaiacol is a benzene ring with an OH and a methoxy group side by side. It forms when wood burns and gives smoked foods their aroma, and phenols like it slow spoilage.

segments.name: Smoked Foods
segments.text: Guaiacol itself isn't a concern; the concern with smoking is the PAHs that come with the smoke. Liquid smoke is filtered, so most PAHs are removed.

figures.title: Curing and Nitrosamines
figures.subtitle: How curing salt can form nitrosamines, and how vitamin C stops it.

segments.name: Nitrite
segments.text: Nitrite is the curing salt from the Additives lesson. It keeps cured meat pink, adds flavor and stops the bacterium that causes botulism.

segments.name: Making a Nitrosamine
segments.text: Amines like dimethylamine come from protein breakdown. In frying heat or stomach acid, nitrite puts an N=O group on the amine's nitrogen, making a nitrosamine. NDMA is the most common one.

segments.name: Nitrosamine Risk
segments.text: Nitrosamines cause cancer in many animal species, and IARC calls NDMA probably carcinogenic. They're thought to be one reason processed meat is classed as carcinogenic to humans, mainly for colorectal cancer. Crisp-fried bacon forms the most.

segments.name: Vitamin C Blocks It
segments.text: Vitamin C, as ascorbate or erythorbate, reacts with nitrite first and blocks the reaction. US rules for bacon require it alongside the nitrite.

segments.name: Uncured and Vegetables
segments.text: Meat labeled uncured is usually cured with celery powder, which bacteria turn into nitrite, so the chemistry is the same. Vegetables are different: they supply most dietary nitrate, along with vitamin C, and are linked to lower cancer risk.

figures.title: Fermentation and Pasteurization
figures.subtitle: Microbes that preserve food, and heat that makes it safe.

segments.name: Lactic Acid
segments.text: Fermentation uses microbes to change food. Lactic acid bacteria turn sugar into lactic acid, which sours milk into yogurt and preserves cabbage as sauerkraut and kimchi.

segments.name: Alcohol, Gas and Vinegar
segments.text: Yeast turns sugar into ethanol and carbon dioxide; in bread the gas raises the dough and the alcohol bakes off. Then Acetobacter bacteria can turn ethanol into acetic acid: vinegar.

segments.name: Why Ferment
segments.text: The acid keeps harmful bacteria from growing, and fermentation can predigest food: yogurt has less lactose, and sourdough less phytate. The things to watch are alcohol and the salt in some ferments.

segments.name: Pasteurization
segments.text: Pasteurization uses just enough heat to kill germs. Most milk is heated to 72 degrees Celsius for 15 seconds; ultra-high temperature milk gets about 135 to 150 degrees for a few seconds and keeps without refrigeration until opened.

segments.name: Why Pasteurize
segments.text: It kills Listeria, Salmonella, E. coli and Campylobacter while barely changing the nutrients. US health agencies warn that raw milk is riskier, especially for children, pregnant women and older adults.

figures.title: Hydrogenation and Refining
figures.subtitle: Firming oils, and stripping grains and oils down.

segments.name: Adding Hydrogen
segments.text: Hydrogenation bubbles hydrogen gas through hot oil with a nickel catalyst. A four-carbon piece stands in for a fatty acid here, with a natural cis double bond.

segments.name: Full or Partial
segments.text: Add both hydrogens and the double bond becomes single: a straight, solid, saturated chain. Stop partway and some double bonds flip to trans instead. That's trans fat, from Figure 7 of the Fats lesson.

segments.name: Trans Fat Rules
segments.text: Industrial trans fat raises LDL and lowers HDL. In 2015 the FDA ruled partially hydrogenated oils no longer generally recognized as safe, and they've been removed from US foods. Fully hydrogenated oil is saturated fat with almost no trans.

segments.name: Refining Grain
segments.text: Refining grain removes the bran and germ, leaving the starchy endosperm. That loses fiber, B vitamins, iron, magnesium, zinc and vitamin E. Enriched flour gets some B vitamins, folic acid and iron back, but not the fiber or the other minerals.

segments.name: Refining Oil
segments.text: Most oils are also refined, bleached and deodorized. That makes them clear, mild and stable for frying, but strips much of their vitamin E and polyphenols. Extra-virgin olive oil and cold-pressed oils skip these steps.

figures.title: Nixtamalization
figures.subtitle: The lime soak that makes corn more nutritious.

segments.name: Lime
segments.text: Nixtamalization starts with slaked lime, calcium hydroxide. In water it breaks into calcium ions and hydroxide, making a strongly alkaline soak.

segments.name: Freeing Niacin
segments.text: In raw corn, niacin, vitamin B3, is tied to other molecules and can't be absorbed. The alkaline soak cuts it free.

segments.name: Other Gains
segments.text: It also loosens the hull, adds calcium, improves the balance of available amino acids, lowers some mold toxins, and lets the dough hold together for tortillas.

segments.name: Pellagra
segments.text: Where corn became a staple without it, in parts of Europe and the US South, pellagra was common: niacin deficiency, with dermatitis, diarrhea and dementia.

segments.name: Corn to Tortilla
segments.text: The steps are simple: cook dried corn with lime, steep it overnight, rinse, and grind into masa. Corn tortillas, tamales and hominy are nixtamalized; cornmeal, grits and polenta usually aren't.

figures.title: Where processed foods act in the body
figures.subtitle: Tap a number on the cell to see what that part does; the list below it gives every other place in the body.

segments.name: Where Processed Foods Act
segments.text: Here's where compounds from cooking and processing act: first inside a single cell, then everywhere else in the body. Some are made by heat, some by curing, and some by refining.
segments.cue: The cell drawing and the list of places

segments.name: Inside a Cell
segments.text: Processing changes what arrives at your cells. High-heat browning makes compounds like acrylamide and AGEs, and charring meat makes heterocyclic amines. The liver's smooth ER processes them, sometimes turning them into forms that can damage DNA. Refining strips some vitamins the mitochondria rely on, which is why many flours are fortified.
segments.cue: The cell drawing and its numbered parts

foodBody.name: Acrylamide
foodBody.text: Forms when starchy foods brown at high heat (fries, toast, chips).

foodBody.name: AGEs
foodBody.text: Form with browning, grilling and roasting; the body also makes them when blood sugar is high.

foodBody.name: Fortification
foodBody.text: Refined flour is often enriched with iron, B vitamins and folic acid.

segments.name: Digestion
segments.text: Cooking softens starch and protein so the small intestine digests them faster, and nixtamalization frees niacin in corn and adds calcium from the lime. In the stomach, nitrite from cured meat can form nitrosamines.
segments.cue: In the list: stomach, small intestine and bones

foodBody.name: Nitrosamines
foodBody.text: Formed from nitrite and amines in cured meats, especially when fried, and in the stomach. Some cause cancer in animals.

segments.name: Liver and Blood Vessels
segments.text: The liver activates and clears acrylamide, HCAs and PAHs, and some of the products can damage DNA, which is why charring and very browned starchy food are best kept moderate. Trans fat from partial hydrogenation raises LDL cholesterol and harms blood vessels. The kidneys clear what's left in urine.
segments.cue: In the list: liver, blood vessels and kidneys

foodBody.name: Acrylamide
foodBody.text: Formed when starchy foods such as fries, chips and toast brown at high heat. The liver turns it into glycidamide, which can damage DNA.

foodBody.name: HCAs and PAHs
foodBody.text: HCAs form in meat cooked very hot, PAHs in smoke and charring. The liver activates and clears both.

segments.name: Fermentation and the Gut
segments.text: Live cultures from yogurt and other fermented foods meet the gut bacteria in the large intestine. Eating a lot of processed meat is linked to colon cancer.
segments.cue: In the list: the large intestine

foodBody.name: Live cultures
foodBody.text: Bacteria such as Lactobacillus in yogurt and kefir. Many die in the stomach, and those that survive pass through the large intestine; most don’t stay there for long.

foodBody.name: Processed meat
foodBody.text: Bacon, ham and sausages, preserved with salt and nitrite. Eating a lot of it is linked to colon cancer.

segments.name: Simplified
segments.text: This is simplified. The amounts in normal diets are small, and the links to disease come from large studies of people, so the list shows where these compounds act, not a measure of harm.

figures.title: Putting It All Together
figures.subtitle: The whole lesson in one table, plus a few extras.

segments.name: One Table
segments.text: Here's the whole lesson in one table: each process, what it does, what forms or changes, the main foods, and what's worth doing.

segments.name: Worth Knowing
segments.text: A few extras. Diets high in ultra-processed foods are linked to obesity and chronic disease, though which features matter is still debated. Frying oil reused many times breaks down. And fast, moist methods like microwaving and pressure-cooking keep more vitamins and form few of these heat compounds.
